Case Study Description: The case centres on the dilemma faced by Sampath Kumar, Principal Secretary of Health in the northeastern state of Meghalaya, as he
strives to reduce the high maternal and infant mortality rates in the region. To address the issue, Kumar implemented a variety of measures,
including the use of data and technology for real-time monitoring of high-risk pregnancies, centralising decision-making at the frontline
worker level, enhancing communication between citizens and the state, fostering cross-functional problem-solving among government
departments, building political support, and addressing systemic gaps.
These efforts resulted in significant progress. However, to fully resolve the challenge, Kumar also needed to address broader societal issues,
such as teenage pregnancies and the lack of family planning.
The case centers on a scheme to expand access to primary health care services under the Indian central government’s flagship Ayushman
Bharat program, a national public health insurance initiative. The scheme aimed to establish 1.5 lakh Health and Wellness Centers across
India to provide free and universal comprehensive primary health care. These centers would offer a wide range of services, including health
and wellness services, maternal and child health services, treatment for non-communicable diseases, palliative and rehabilitative care, oral,
eye, ENT, mental health, elderly care, and emergency and trauma care.
The program manager encountered several challenges in implementing this ambitious project. Key obstacles included obtaining approval to
recruit a new cadre of officers, namely Community Health Officers, to serve in these centers. Additionally, there were significant efforts
required in capacity building and training these officers and other primary health service personnel, as well as monitoring the performance
and effectiveness of these centers.
This case focuses on JEEViKA, Bihar’s Rural Livelihoods Promotion Society, an initiative aimed at organizing economically marginalized
women in the state into self-help groups. These groups empower women to seek employment opportunities and access funding. One
notable program conceptualized under JEEViKA is the “Didi ki Rasoi” initiative. Through this program, local women establish institutional
canteens at state hospitals, schools, and other community centers to provide fresh, home-cooked healthy meals. This initiative addresses
the issue of poor food quality in these institutions while simultaneously generating employment and income for the women involved.
The case revolves around Dr. Shahid Iqbal Choudhary, an IAS Officer in Jammu and Kashmir, who faces the challenge of high youth
unemployment and disenfranchisement in the state. In response, Dr. Shahid launched the Mission Youth initiative in March 2021 with the
goal of transforming the state's youth into ambassadors of peace, prosperity, and development. This initiative included a series of
interventions aimed at improving employment, empowerment, and engagement among the youth, securing Rs. 200 crores in state funds for
the program. The program was a resounding success, resulting in a significant increase in job creation and youth engagement.
The case is situated in Wayanad, a Northern district in the state of Kerala, where the scheduled tribe (ST) community comprises a high share
of the local population, yet is economically marginalised. The local officer in charge, Mr. Nair, comes up with an innovative way to generate

model heritage village – a tourist site in which tribes can be employed while generating revenues for themselves and the district. He puts in
place training programs to ensure that ST members are able to contribute to the project.
The Rewa Solar Project (RUMSL) case offers an authoritative example of public-private partnerships in India and helps discern how risk can
be mitigated to ensure the success of a PPP model. An innovation by IAS Manu Srivastava, Rewa was financed in a way to ensure that the
project did not rely on viable gap funding (VGF), offered by the Government of India while attracting procurers. RUMSL was commissioned

the beginning, Manu Srivastava faced a spectrum of challenges such as identifying donors, maintaining an attractive tariff rate without VGF,
acquiring land, and identifying procurers. By studying these challenges and the solutions adopted by Manu Srivastava, learners can learn the
innovative ways through which risk can be mitigated in a large project such as RUMSL.
The Madhya Pradesh solar rooftop installation case is a good example to illustrate how to make a project an attractive proposition for key
stakeholders. The case can help us understand how de-risking a project, addressing information asymmetry, mitigating risks, and ensuring
transparency in the project cycle drives increased and informed participation.The case unfolds against the challenge of increasing solar

Case Study Title: case of Rewa Solar Rooftop Installation
Case Study Description: rooftop installations to meet the state’s solar energy production targets under the National Solar Mission. Mr Manu Srivastava, head of
Madhya Pradesh Urja Vikas Nigam Limited, is tasked with resolving the puzzle of why uptake is low despite incentives offered by the
government. Through addressing key stakeholder concerns, efficient project structuring, and process innovations in a market-based
financing model, the climate agenda is taken forward.
The development and implementation of Rail Divyang Saarthi application by the Ahmedabad Division of Western Railways is a good case to
discuss embedding technology into policy solutions effectively for People with Disabilities (PwD). The app helped significantly reduce the
number of days applicants had to wait to receive their railway concession cards. Accessibility and inclusion are the principles that resurface
throughout this story. It demonstrates how technology is not a one-stop solution and how its effectiveness goes hand-in-hand with clarity in
policies, inter-departmental coordination and communication. The app helped significantly reduce the number of days applicants had to
wait to receive their railway concession cards.
The Rail Madad Application of Indian Railways is a good case to discuss principles of decentralisation and transparency in large-scale
grievance redressal systems. It uses a passenger or benefactor-centric model to achieve maximum customer satisfaction. To create this
system, they focus on a bottom-up approach with room for levels of escalation, ensuring speedy service delivery while maintaining full
transparency across the board. Rail Madad is the brainchild of Vivek Srivastava, the protagonist of the innovation. Soon after joining the
commercial department of Rail Bhawan in New Delhi, Srivastava discovered that the many channels of communication established by
divisions across the country were not standardised or centralised to provide real-time grievance redressal for the passengers. He led his
team to create a singular platform, Rail Madad, that connected passengers to the last-mile service delivery staff to offer real-time problem
resolution while offering full transparency to all stakeholders.
The ASTR case illustrates the administrative and ethical complexities of employing AI-based facial recognition powered solutions for
governance. The case unfolds against terrorism concerns in J&K in 2021. Around the same time, the Department of Telecommunications
(DoT) under Mr. Naveen Jakhar was working on addressing the increase in cybercrime in Mewat, Haryana, due to the issue of SIM cards

Case Study Title: Leveraging AI for Security: The case of
Case Study Description: based on fake identities.
The use of fake SIM cards is leveraged to propose a solution based on adopting AI-based facial recognition technology to identify fake SIM
cards. The case can help us understand how an ecosystem could be developed, to facilitate the smooth interaction of stakeholders needed
to incorporate facial recognition technology in governance.
The ‘Nature Retreat and Awareness Camp’ – an ecotourism project in Chamrod, Dhar Kalan in Punjab – is a good case to discuss the
principles of participatory natural resource management. The relevant principles include understanding natural resources management
mechanism, biodiversity of the ecosystem, livelihood strategies sustained by the ecosystem, and participatory environmental governance.
The case set between 2017 and to present day in Chamrod, Dhar Kalan in Punjab was developed in 2017 where Dr Sanjeev Kumar, the
protagonist undertakes the task of efficiently using the barren land near the Ranjit Sagar Lake to help bring about economic development in
the Dhar Kalan’s villages. Being cognizant of the fact that such ecotourism camp in an ecologically sensitive zone requires a scientific
approach, careful planning and participatory support from local residents to assure the sustainability of the ecosystem. Conserving Dhar
forest's flora and fauna and spreading awareness about green living to people residing were essential elements to the project’s
development.
The establishment of an IT Cell in the Chief Commercial Manager (Passenger) office in the Southern Railways is an ideal case to discuss
principles of optimal utilisation of limited resources in team building. Relevant principles include capacity building through continuous
guided learning, adaptive management through the institutionalisation of innovation, committed leadership and responsive governance.The
case is set in December 2017 when Mr. Vinayan was appointed as the Chief Commercial Manager (Passenger) of Southern Railways,
headquartered in Chennai. With decades of experience in Southern Railways, Mr. Vinayan is aware of challenges that affect the efficiency of

Case Study Title: The case of the IT Cell initiative

Case Study Description: the system for both its employees and passengers. He knows that the solutions to these challenges can be through technological
development, but he does not want to outsource the work to external agencies and become dependent on their service. He undertakes the
charge to address these challenges internally by developing an IT Cell, using old resources that already exist and harnessing those lying
dormant.
The pond rejuvenation project in Udham Singh Nagar, Uttarakhand is a good case to discuss the principles of applying an ecosystem
approach to governance. Relevant principles include focusing on relationships and processes within the ecosystem of key players' economic
and political activity, benefit-sharing, adaptive and responsive management, including change management practices, appropriate
decentralisation of tasks and responsibilities, and intersectoral cooperation. The case is set between 2019 and present-day Udham Singh
Nagar, Uttrakhand, where Mayur Dixit, the protagonist, undertakes the task of rejuvenating ponds that have been encroached upon to
recharge the district’s groundwater table. Apart from hydrogeological reasons, Udham Singh Nagar, a district located in Uttarakhand’s Terai
region, is on the verge of a general water crisis resulting from water-intensive farming and rampant industrialisation. Mayur Dixit is aware of
the limits of simply recharging ponds via desilting and other conventional pond rejuvenation methods. He understands the need to develop
a holistic approach that takes into account the underlying causes of the lowered groundwater levels.
The Har Ghar Tikakaran campaign is centred on the remarkable efforts of Dr. Veena Dhawan and her dedicated team, who spearheaded one
of the largest vaccination drives ever conducted in India - the National Covid-19 Vaccination Program, amidst the throes of a pandemic. This
campaign reflects upon the myriad challenges and obstacles encountered by the team and illuminates their triumphant journey in
surmounting these hurdles through unwavering unity, unyielding determination, and exemplary cooperation.
In rural India, Lekhpals are crucial in safeguarding property rights and facilitating various administrative tasks. Despite their significance,
there has been a lack of an objective performance management system to track their effectiveness. This deficiency hinders the
government's ability to identify strong performers, support those needing improvement, and ensure accountability. To address this, UP
Govt. developed a comprehensive performance management system named LAKSHYAM (Lekhpals Actionable KPI System for Holistic
Assessment and Management) and piloted it in Prayagraj. LAKSHYAM operates on three pillars: Objective KPIs, Direct Supervisor Feedback,
and Stakeholders & Feedback.
Ms. Tejaswi Satpute, Mumbai's Deputy Commissioner of Police spearheaded Operation Parivartan, targeting the long-standing issue of illicit
liquor consumption in Solapur, rooted in illegal brewing and hazardous ingredients. Facing challenges in conventional raids, Ms. Tejaswi
adopted a scientific strategy to address the entire brewing cycle, aiming to disrupt the production and distribution of illicit liquor. The 72-
hour brewing cycle was a critical focus, requiring post-raid actions for a lasting solution. Her dedication to ethical principles in public service
guided her efforts to combat the multifaceted issues associated with the illicit liquor trade.
Kathirimalai, a remote tribal hamlet in Erode district of Tamil Nadu, was inaccessible due to its location on a high mountain top in the Bargur
Hills and deep within the Channampatti forest reserve. Also, home to 400 members of the Sholaga tribe, these inhabitants of Kathirimalai
Village needed to travel several hours along a rough trail and through the forest to access medical facilities at the nearest primary health
centre. Severe malnutrition, stunting, and communicable diseases were prevalent among these tribals as they mostly avoided visiting the
medical centre for regular health reviews. Even the availability of educational facilities in a single-teacher local school was minimal. Poor
learning outcomes and absenteeism among school-going children was common.
A young IAS officer, Mr. Krishnanunni led a coordinated effort under Project Punnagai (Project Smile) to transform this hamlet. The Wi-Fi
facility, set up in the school premises, essentially to establish telemedicine facilities in Kathirimalai was used as a convergence platform to
bring other facilities to the community viz., learning resources for improving education, skill development programs for enhancing
employability of youth, livelihood enhancement by better agriculture and animal rearing practices. Today Project Punnagai is being
replicated across multiple villages of Tamil Nadu.
The Delhi Development Authority (DDA), as a regulatory body, is responsible for the management of land resources under the Master Plan
for Delhi, India’s capital city. It controls the planning, acquisition, development, and allotment of land for private, public, and government
needs. Following his appointment as Commissioner (Land Disposal), Mr. Subu recognised an urgent need to develop a digital information
system for the effective processing and management of land records and activities. Previous efforts by DDA to implement digitalisation
through data outsourcing to leading software development companies had failed and tracking documents was difficult. Mr. Subu initiated
the development of the information system named Initiative for Digitalisation of Land Information (IDLI), which is an online cloud-managed
information system for the workflow of land-related activities. It provides transparency and improved turnaround time for service delivery.
The case highlights the positive impacts of Leadership Intervention and Succession Planning at HPCL through Various Strategies- T20
Strategy, T25 Strategy, HP Possible Model. All these interventions were focused on identifying, training and skilling the potential leaders in
the company for a smooth succession and seamless working of the company.
The Chikkaballapur district administration in Karnataka was working hard to scale up COVID-19 vaccinations, but without much success.

one behind. Following an understanding of the causes underlying vaccine resistance and implementation challenges in the district,
appropriate measures were undertaken to raise awareness and design effective vaccine delivery systems.
NALC is a Free of Cost Service which enables flexible, state of the art, futuristic and leisure learning space which enables people from all age
groups to learn and improve every aspect of their personality through free Wi-Fi (24x7), online training through tablets, e-reading through
kindle, etc, in an environment furnished with modular furniture. It converges resources that are rendered unused viz. libraries of

Case Study Title: the lives of the students of Changlang
Case Study Description: government schools are marred with a lack of dedicated library teachers, library infrastructure and books and transforms these existing
libraries into NALC helping in optimum utilisation of unused resources of libraries run by the library department which acts as cluster
libraries for nearby schools wherein children from all schools may access this space as their library.
This case documents the innovative and collaborative efforts by the Bijnor administration to create wealth from the bicycles—abandoned
by the migrant workers during the COVID-19 pandemic—to birth the inclusive Bikes of Bijnor ride-sharing program. The bicycles left as a
heap of iron waste outside the police stations of Bijnor in Uttar Pradesh were utilised in the ridesharing program with significant social and
environmental benefit. Under the program, the bicycle owners were first identified and then compensated to obtain legal possession of the
bicycles. Bicycles were then refurbished, and bike stands were set up at 10 spots in Bijnor town. The bicycles were then made available for

Case Study Title: Bikes of Bijnor: A waste to wealth public

Case Study Description: hire at a minimal cost.
The ridesharing program—the brainchild of the Bijnor Joint Magistrate, Mr. Vikramaditya Singh Malik, in 2020-21—brought together the
civil service and the municipal administration. Both collaborated to fund the project and formally registered “Bikes of Bijnor “as a society
headed by the Sub-divisional Magistrate (SDM) Sadar, while the Head and the Executive Officer of the Nagar Palika functioned as its
secretary.
In the heart of Gujarat, the transformative impact of cadaver organ transplantation unfolds through powerful narratives. These stories
highlight the profound effect of the State Organ and Tissue Transplantation Organisation (SOTTO), established in 2019 to revolutionise
cadaver organ procurement and transplantation across government and private hospitals. Guided by rigorous protocols and the 2020 Brain
Stem Death Declaration guidelines, SOTTO ensures ethical and efficient practices. Its online platform, launched in May 2020, enhances
transparency and coordination, matching organs with recipients to maximise life-saving impacts. These efforts underscore Gujarat's
commitment to fostering a sustainable healthcare ecosystem through the generosity of donors, breathing hope and life into countless
individuals.
The case revolves around Andhra Pradesh Transmission Corporation (APTransco) efforts to advance India's electricity grid management with
the introduction of the country's inaugural AI-driven day-ahead electricity forecasting model. This innovation predicts electricity
consumption and demand in precise 15-minute intervals, thus optimises grid operations, minimising costs, and extends its forecasting
capabilities to include wind, solar energy, and market prices. With an aim to establish a low-cost dispatch model for electricity generation,
APTransco underlines its commitment to efficient grid management.
The Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB) launched an innovative Vehicle Location Tracking System (VLTS) developed in collaboration with
NIC Gujarat and NIC Uttarakhand to enhance the monitoring and management of hazardous waste transportation. This project aims to

Case Study Title: Vehicle Tracking to Ensure Cradle to

Case Study Description: ensure the safe and compliant movement of hazardous materials by leveraging advanced GPS technology, real-time tracking, and robust
data analytics. By implementing the VLTS, GPCB seeks to mitigate environmental risks, improve regulatory oversight and promote

Case Study Title: Disposal of Hazardous Waste in Gujarat

Case Study Description: sustainable waste management practices across the state. This case study delves into the technical aspects, implementation challenges and
anticipated benefits of this groundbreaking initiative, underscoring its potential to set new standards in environmental regulation.
Dr. Debajit Mahanta and his team, aimed at uplifting the socio-economic status of the tribal population through bioresource-based
entrepreneurship. Leveraging the state's rich biodiversity, the CoE, supported by various national and international institutions, focuses on
research, innovation, and capacity building to create sustainable livelihoods and promote economic growth. It addresses challenges like
unemployment and limited market access, striving to preserve cultural identity while adapting to modern advancements. The initiative
exemplifies a holistic approach to biodiversity conservation, sustainable development, and techno-economic empowerment, aspiring to

Case Study Title: A Case Study from Arunachal Pradesh

Case Study Description: serve as a model for the entire Northeast region of the country.
In the past few years, Odisha has emerged as a hub for sporting activities in India. It has hosted international sporting events such as the
Asian Athletics Championship (2017) and two hockey World Cups (2018 and 2023), besides having built the largest seated hockey stadium in
the world and laid 22 artificial hockey turfs in a single district. By the end of 2023, Odisha had 90 multi-purpose indoor stadiums, 25 hockey
training centres, 314 rural mini stadiums and 149 urban mini stadiums . During the same period, there was a significant increase in Odisha
state’s representation in national and international sports events, improvement in athlete performance besides large-scale participation
from the grassroots in numerous sports disciplines. Odisha’s transformation as a leader in sports was led by a multitude of factors such as
an inspired and involved leadership, a committed bureaucracy and a well-orchestrated public-private partnership that complemented each
other. This case study covers in depth how multitude actors from diverse organisations and institutions came together to create an
ecosystem of sporting excellence in Odisha, which has hitherto never been seen in India.
The Land Resource Inventory (LRI) was developed as a new approach to enhance the impact of the watershed programme. It is an inventory
of five physical factors—rock, soil, slope, erosion type and severity and vegetation—which form the basis for assessing land resources. The
Land Resource Inventory (LRI) technology—developed under Sujala III in 2013-14 and implemented in 11 districts—empowers farmers with
site-specific information to make crop choices and boost farm incomes.
It was designed for execution through a consortium of partners to develop a site-specific land resource database through use of state-of-
the-art remote sensing (RS) and geographic information systems for data collection and interpretation. A Land Resources Portal for
information dissemination was then established by developing a digital library through pooling all the spatial and non-spatial data,
containing both site-specific farm information and generalised data about land. A mobile application was developed to enable farmers to
access the LRI portal. The Watershed Development Department (WDD) of the Karnataka state government spearheaded the project.
The case explores how the multiple stakeholders in the GST project were finally able to work together to implement GST. How is consensus
built when so many parties are involved? How are the diverse interests of these stakeholders safeguarded in the process? The case also
examines the complexities of the Indian taxation system pre-GST and thus, delves into the inherent consequent complexity of such a

Case Study Title: GST: The Story of India’s biggest tax

Case Study Description: massive tax reform as GST. How did the centre get the states on board with the idea of GST? How was a rapport of trust and understanding
established between the centre and the states? Finally, the case looks briefly at the challenge of bringing a new technology-driven system
into a nation that was just beginning to accustom itself to the concept of digitalization. The case explores how all these factors tied in to
making GST possible, and a major success, at that.
This case study highlights the innovative approach of Ms. Varnali Dekha in addressing nutrition-related challenges faced by children in
Kokrajhar district, Assam. Under the broader “Poshan” initiative, Ms. Dekha employs a multifaceted six-pronged strategy designed to tackle
these issues comprehensively. Her approach integrates various creative interventions aimed at improving nutritional outcomes, enhancing
community awareness, and fostering sustainable practices. Through this case study, we explore the effectiveness of her strategies and their
impact on the well-being of children in the region, providing valuable insights into the practical application of targeted nutritional
interventions.
This case explores the Indian Space Research Organisation’s (ISRO) landmark achievement with Chandrayaan-3, which made India the first
country to land near the lunar South Pole on August 23, 2023. It highlights the strategic leadership, structured failure analysis, and risk
management that defined the mission — along with ISRO’s hallmark strengths in cost-effective innovation, organizational culture, and a
balanced approach to collaboration and self-reliance. The case offers insights into how ISRO’s inclusive, learning-driven ecosystem enabled
a bold leap in space exploration, setting the stage for even more ambitious missions ahead.
India’s agriculture sector continues to be a mainstay of the country’s economy, supporting millions of livelihoods and is the backbone of
rural development. Despite its importance, the sector continues to be plagued by poor public investments, limited access and uptake of
technology, and outdated practices. The Raj Kisan Sathi Portal is a novel effort by the Government of Rajasthan to modernise agricultural
practices in the state using IT solutions. Initiated in 2019, the portal simplifies farming processes, provides vital information, and improves
service delivery for farmers. In this policy and technology integration case, students will learn about the design, implementation, and
challenges associated with executing and scaling a state-wide initiative. Studying this initiative offers valuable insights into leveraging
technology to address systemic challenges in the agricultural sector to improve efficiency and social equity.
The PM SVANidhi Scheme has emerged as a catalyst for inclusive urban entrepreneurship, breaking barriers that previously limited access
for marginalized micro-entrepreneurs. With a notable rise in female participation, the scheme has advanced women’s entrepreneurial
empowerment, contributing to broader gender equality in urban markets. PM SVANidhi has strengthened the sustainability of small urban
businesses. This caselet explores the scheme’s implementation, the challenges faced in reaching its objectives and outlines the path ahead
to further enhance its role in fostering resilient and inclusive urban livelihoods.
Micro enterprises play a critical role in India’s economy, contributing to GDP, exports, and job creation. However, over 99% operate
informally, limiting access to finance and government benefits. To address this, the Ministry of MSME launched Udyam Registration in 2020,
but many informal micro enterprises (IMEs) remained unregistered due to lack of awareness, documents, and digital skills. To bridge this
gap, the Ministry introduced the Udyam Assist Platform (UAP) on January 11, 2023, developed and managed by SIDBI. Unlike the self-
registration Udyam Registration Portal, UAP enables banks and microfinance institutions to register IMEs on their behalf, using Aadhaar-
based verification and bulk data uploads. The platform enhances reach, ensures data security, and issues an Udyam Assist Certificate,
allowing IMEs to later self-register fully.
The Pradhan Mantri PVTG Mission, a flagship program of the Indian Government, is dedicated to enhance the socio-economic conditions of
the Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) in the country. This case delves into the assessment and resolution of challenges faced by
the mission, which has been allocated a budget of Rs. 15,000 crore over three years, commencing in 2023-24. The mission aims to provide
critical support in the form of housing, water, sanitation, education, healthcare, and livelihood opportunities, while respecting the cultural
integrity of PVTGs. This case offers a comprehensive understanding of the issues faced by PVTGs, and the effectiveness of the mission in
addressing these concerns, aligning with broader governmental objectives in accordance with United Nation’s Sustainable Development
Goals (UNSDGs). The case encourages adoption of an empathetic approach and devising of impact-oriented execution strategies.
On April 25, 2022, Mr. Arun Mehta, Principal Chief Materials Manager of Western Railways, launched a transformative Third-Party
Inspection (TPI) initiative to modernize quality assurance in Indian Railways. The program aimed to enhance efficiency, build capacity, and
create a competitive inspection ecosystem focused on quality over cost. Presented to top Railway Board officials, it received strong support
from the Chairman, Member Finance, and RDSO. On May 8, 2022, the Board authorized Western Railway to engage private TPI agencies for
2–3 years. Tasked with designing the empanelment system, Mr. Mehta sought to integrate private efficiencies without disrupting
inspections while reflecting on fairness and possible stakeholder conflicts.
A retired senior civil servant, living a quiet post-service life, drew attention when the Benami Unit in Delhi spotted unusual property records.
Quiet checks began—silent, precise, unnoticed. Clues pointed to hidden wealth. A secret search was planned across four cities. When the
Income Tax teams struck, they uncovered a web of unreported assets and benami properties worth over ₹240 crores. Behind the calm
facade lay a story of evasion—now exposed.
This case study explores the institutionalization of Tithi Bhojan under the PM POSHAN scheme as a model of community-led action to
address child malnutrition. It highlights the shift from government-led service delivery to community-enabled participation, examining how
diverse stakeholders collaborate to integrate the initiative into policy. The case raises key questions about sustaining community

Case Study Title: Case Study of the Tithi Bhojan Initiative
Case Study Description: engagement, building multi-stakeholder partnerships, and embedding participatory governance in public nutrition programs for long-term
impact.
This case explores the ambitious digital transformation of the Human Resources function in Indian Railways, one of the largest public sector
employers in the world. It follows the shift from a manual, paper-based system to an integrated Human Resource Management System
(HRMS) developed by CRIS, the IT arm of Indian Railways. The case outlines why the change was needed, how it was implemented, and the
challenges faced along the way, from managing legacy data and ensuring cybersecurity to handling change in a hierarchical system. It also
touches on stakeholder engagement, training, and the wider impact of digitisation in government. This is a story of transforming scale with
strategy, and legacy with leadership.
India’s long-standing battle against Kala-azar persisted despite substantial resources and strategic programmes under NKEP. In 2021, Mr.
Rajiv Manjhi identified that program success hinged on behavioural change and direct community involvement. Through innovative, locally
adapted solutions—such as mud-house crack sealing, intensified surveillance, targeted vector management, health worker training, and
rural evening awareness sessions—the programme enhanced effectiveness and public engagement. These measures significantly
strengthened disease control efforts and marked a pivotal shift toward achieving national Kala-azar elimination.
This case study showcases the transformation of 20 Scheduled Tribe families in Ganori Gram Panchayat who, after years of living in forest
encroachments without housing rights, gained secure homes through collective action. Led by Sarpanch Mrs. Saralataai Tandale, with
support from the Block Development Officer, DRDA Project Director Ms. Sangeetadevi Patil, and others, land was purchased under the
Pandit Dindayal Upadhyay Gharkul Scheme. Villager Mr. Dadasaheb Jadhav sold 20 gunthas at a fair rate, and Ms. Anuradha Chavan covered
registration costs. Using MGNREGA labour, houses were built with sanitation, LPG, and tap water under national schemes. The initiative
demonstrates how convergence between local leadership and administration fosters inclusion, dignity, and lasting empowerment.
Odisha revitalized India’s flagship skill development program, DDU-GKY, which initially struggled with low enrolment, weak awareness, and
high dropouts. The Odisha Rural Development and Marketing Society (ORMAS) introduced a structured mobilization model by incentivizing
Community Cadres (Gram Rojgar Sevaks, Community Resource Persons, Master Book Keepers) and using mobilisation camps, IEC tools, and

Case Study Title: Cadres for Rural Youth Engagement in

Case Study Description: community engagement. This approach boosted enrolment, improved training outcomes, and enhanced job retention, demonstrating how
community-driven strategies can make national missions more effective.
The case study examines the impact of Mission Shakti, a government initiative launched in Odisha, India, to promote women-led
entrepreneurship and empowerment. The programme has enabled women to engage in income-generating activities, access financial
services, and build leadership skills. It has strengthened women’s self-help groups (SHGs) through capacity building, skill development, and
financial inclusion. Mission Shakti has empowered women to start and scale businesses, boosting their confidence, financial independence,
and participation in social and political spheres. It further emphasizes the importance of community support, policy backing, and sustainable
practices in ensuring long-term success, positioning Mission Shakti as a potential model for broader replication.
The Asomi Pearl Farming Project in Nagaon, Assam, demonstrates how grassroots innovation can enhance rural livelihoods by integrating
freshwater pearl cultivation with traditional aquaculture, creating additional income streams and environmental benefits. Despite technical
and market challenges, the initiative succeeded through skill development, cooperative financial support, and buy-back assurances. With
the global pearl market exceeding USD 10.5 billion and India’s presence still limited, the project highlights Assam’s potential to become a
key player in global pearl value chains. Scaling the model will require advanced training, improved grafting techniques, stronger cooperative
governance, branding, and policy-backed market linkages, enabling its transformation into a sustainable, market-driven rural enterprise that
strengthens economic resilience.
India, home to over 6,000 large dams—many aging and vulnerable—faced longstanding challenges in ensuring dam safety due to
fragmented practices and federal complexities. The 1979 Machchhu-2 dam disaster underscored the urgency, but legislative efforts stalled
for decades. The Dam Safety Act, 2021 marks a historic shift by establishing a uniform, legally binding framework for dam safety across

Case Study Title: India's Dam Safety Act: From Risk to
Case Study Description: India. Overcoming constitutional hurdles, inter-state tensions, and institutional inertia, the Act was enabled by sustained bureaucratic
advocacy, legal innovation, and broad stakeholder engagement. Key features include a four-tier safety structure, mandatory inspections,
real-time monitoring, and clear accountability mechanisms—balancing national oversight with state autonomy. This case highlights how
long-term reform is possible through persistence, adaptive policymaking, and cooperative federalism. It offers lessons for future legislation
involving complex governance and public safety systems.
This case presents the policy design and implementation journey of MJPSKY, Maharashtra’s flagship farm loan waiver scheme (2019–20),
crafted in response to the operational failures of an earlier waiver (CSMSSY, 2017). The case offers a comparative study of two state-led

Case Study Title: From Crisis to Championing: The Story
Case Study Description: interventions and explores themes of administrative reform, welfare technology, crisis management, and institutional accountability. It

verification model, phased rollout, direct government control of IT systems, and behavioral incentives for credit discipline. Ideal for

This case study examines how Visakhapatnam Port Authority (VPA) achieved a remarkable turnaround by entering the World Bank’s Global
Top 20 Container Port Performance Index (CPPI) in 2024, rising from rank 115 to 19 within a year. Located strategically on India’s eastern
seaboard near the Malacca Strait, VPA leveraged strong rail-road connectivity to strengthen its competitive position. The transformation
was led by Chairperson Dr. M. Angamuthu, appointed in May 2023, at a time when the port faced ageing infrastructure, procedural delays,
and intense competition from private ports. Using the autonomy provided by the Major Port Authorities Act, 2021, the leadership
implemented reforms focused on operational efficiency, digitalization, and stakeholder coordination. A long-standing PPP with Visakha
Container Terminal Pvt. Ltd., along with ecosystem-wide collaboration, enabled capacity upgrades, improved turnaround times, and greater
environmental sustainability.
In Dec 2022, the Government of India launched the Digi Yatra initiative at three airports (Delhi, Bengaluru, Varanasi)—a first-of-its-kind
digital transformation program that aimed to streamline air travel processes and enhance passenger experiences at airports across the
country. The program aimed to eliminate long queues, reduce paperwork, and improve security checks by leveraging biometric technology
and digital identification. The Airports Authority of India (AAI), along with other airport operators, took on the task of implementing this
ambitious project. Starting with three airports, the government rolled out the initiative in a phased manner, and by the end of 2024, it had
implemented Digi Yatra across various airports in the country, significantly improving passenger convenience and operational efficiency.
In a landmark reform, the Government of India restructured the century-old Ordnance Factory Board (OFB) into seven Defence Public Sector
Undertakings (DPSUs) on October 1, 2021, to tackle longstanding inefficiencies in defence production. Triggered by repeated CAG reports
and expert committee recommendations, the move aimed to improve agility, accountability, and responsiveness to the Armed Forces’
needs. Within this transformation, the Chief General Manager of Ordnance Factory Balangir (OFBL), Shri P.K. Dash, faces a key challenge:
enhancing output without compromising on quality or safety, requiring strategic, balanced decision-making.
PARAM Shavak is an indigenous high-performance computing (HPC) desktop system developed under the National Supercomputing Mission
by CDAC, MeitY, and VVDN Technologies. Powered by Rudra, it represents a major step forward in making advanced supercomputing
accessible to academic and research institutions across India. Compact, energy-efficient, and cost-effective, PARAM Shavak enables
institutions with limited resources to undertake cutting-edge research. By democratizing access to HPC, it helps overcome challenges such
as low awareness, funding limitations, and a shortage of skilled professionals. This case study explores the system’s development,
implementation challenges, and its contribution to strengthening India’s research ecosystem and advancing digital transformation.

Chandigarh's ICCC was conceived to combat growing environmental issues such as air pollution, traffic congestion, water scarcity, and poor
waste management. With strong leadership and support under the Smart Cities Mission, the city implemented a technology-driven, data-
integrated command center to monitor and optimize urban operations across 25+ services. It evolved through four phases: planning,
infrastructure development, real-time integration, and community engagement. The case presents both achievements and challenges—
ranging from institutional resistance, financial limitations, and privacy concerns to remarkable successes in traffic management, pollution
control, and citizen participation.

access for Self-Help Groups (SHGs) facing challenges like limited reach, poor quality control, and weak linkages. Through eSARAS.in, SHG

This case study explores how the Department of Telecommunications in India addressed critical Right of Way (RoW) issues hindering
telecom infrastructure expansion at state level between 2021 and 2023. The Licensed Telecom Service providers and Infrastructure
Providers faced significant delays, complex procedures, exorbitant charges, and non-uniform RoW policies across various Indian states. The

Yantra India Limited (YIL), formed in 2021 from eight Ordnance Factories, aimed to boost India’s defence manufacturing but faced major
hurdles in its transition from a government setup to a corporate entity. With limited orders, a ₹1230 million loss, and low employee morale,
the company struggled to stay afloat. The end of overtime pay, manpower shortages, and financial strain deepened challenges. YIL secured
a small order from Indian Railways and credit from SBI but needed stronger momentum. Its leadership now faces critical choices—whether
to expand exports, diversify products, or enhance customer ties—while motivating employees and balancing cost control with welfare to
ensure long-term survival.
A quiet revolution had taken India by storm and reshaped how the Government of India transferred benefits under its welfare programmes
directly to the intended beneficiaries. In India’s fertilizer sector, the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) system had introduced a more transparent
and accountable model for subsidy distribution. Under this system, the government disbursed fertilizer subsidies to companies after the
actual sale of subsidized fertilizers to farmers by retailers. Farmers were identified using Aadhaar-based authentication at the point of sale,
ensuring that benefits reached the intended recipients while minimizing diversion and lowering administrative costs.

column3: This case examines the revitalization of spring water sources and the transformation of a tribal village—Sibbe, situated in Arunachal
Pradesh's Ziro Valley—through integrated water resource management, community engagement, and the convergence of government
schemes, including the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM). The protagonist, Smt. Tage Yani, a grassroots leader, mobilizes the community amid
ecological stress and water scarcity, ushering in sustainable water governance practices. The narrative documents challenges including
deforestation, declining spring flows, community resistance to water tariffs, and lack of technical expertise, and shows how they were
overcome through participative planning, spring shed rejuvenation, capacity-building, and institutional innovations such as Village Water &
Sanitation Committee (VWSC) empowerment and water pricing models.
This case examines the transformation of forest fire management at Bandipur Tiger Reserve (2020–2023) following devastating fires in
2019. The Karnataka Forest Department adopted an innovative community-based model that redefined local communities as conservation
partners rather than threats. Addressing challenges such as climate vulnerability, invasive Lantana camara, limited resources, and strained
community relations, the initiative combined volunteer fire watchers, early warning systems, indigenous knowledge, livelihood-linked
Lantana removal, economic incentives, and capacity building. The results were significant: fire incidents fell by 63%, burned area reduced by
74%, response time dropped sharply, and alternative livelihoods were created for hundreds of families. The case demonstrates that
sustainable conservation depends on community participation, shared economic benefits, and integrating local knowledge with modern
governance tools.
The case study describes the transformation of Kanfodi village in drought-prone Jalna District from distress migration and poverty to a
source of local employment within a decade. Before 2018, households relied only on rainfed crops and faced seasonal migration, poor
infrastructure, and socio-economic hardship. Intervention by MSRLM through SHG formation and financial literacy led to the introduction of
vegetable farming, which became a turning point due to steady income and reliable markets. Innovations like drip irrigation, staggered
planting, and market surveys increased productivity and earnings. Distress migration reduced to 20% by 2024-25, living standards improved,
and women emerged as key decision-makers. Landless households were supported through poultry, goat rearing, and a daal mill. Despite
challenges like water scarcity and institutional gaps, Kanfodi stands as a model of community-led, sustainable rural development.
